2.4 Generating network topology with OpenAI
Show me a network engineer and I will show you an engineer who spends countless hours putting
together network diagrams, drawing lines to illustrate connection points, and even trying to pick
the color scheme that matches their artistic taste. If this sounds like you, you will like this recipe.
In this recipe, we will demonstrate how to automatically generate network topology using Ope-
nAI’s LLM. Traditional topology generation relies heavily on both the engineer’s network knowl-
edge and their familiarity with tools. If the engineer is used to Visio diagrams or draw.io, those
are probably the tools they will use. However, we can use OpenAI to automatically generate
a network topology diagram by interpreting the topology description and producing code for
visualization purposes.
Getting ready
We will use several Python packages to complete this recipe. Please install the following packages
in your virtual environment:
$ sudo apt-get install graphviz
OpenAI Recipes for Network Engineers 54
How to do it…
1. First, we need to give a topology description to OpenAI and generate a Graphviz dot file.
We will name this script recipe_4_01.generate_dot.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Simple script to generate a fat-tree topology dot file using OpenAI
"""
import openai
import os
# Setup OpenAI
client = openai.OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv('OPENAI_API_KEY'))
# Generate dot file content
prompt = """Generate a Graphviz DOT file for a fat-tree network
topology:
- 2 Core routers: core1, core2
- 4 Spine routers: spine1, spine2, spine3, spine4
- 8 Leaf routers: leaf1, leaf2, leaf3, leaf4, leaf5, leaf6, leaf7,
leaf8
Each core connects to all spines, each spine connects to all leaves.
Use different colors for each router type. Return only the DOT file
content."""
response = client.chat.completions.create(
model="gpt-4",
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
temperature=0.3
)
# Extract and save dot file content
content = response.choices[0].message.content
# Find the actual DOT content (between graph/digraph and the closing
brace)

2.5 Generating methods of procedure (MOPs) with
OpenAI
Any network engineer working in a medium to large-sized enterprise environment is probably
familiar with the MOP document. The MOP is generally a detailed document outlining the steps
for executing a specific task or process, often used in network engineering operations. An example
would be a MOP to create a new VLAN, find an available IP block to be used with the VLAN, and
then assign a gateway IP to the VLAN interface.
The MOP focuses on the technical aspect of the process and is often used in a form of knowledge
transfer between senior to junior engineers, or just as a simple reminder of steps when a sleepy
engineer is performing the task at 3 A.M. While the MOP is useful, creating it can be pretty boring.
In this recipe, we will show you how to leverage OpenAI LLMs to help you create one.
Getting ready
We just need the openai Python package for this recipe.

cedures:

prompt engineering. See you there!

Prompt Engineering for
Reliable Outputs
In the previous two chapters, we saw how we can leverage AI LLMs to answer many questions
and help with daily tasks. By now, we know a big part of working with AI LLMs is how we “ask”
AI for what we need. For example, in Chapter 1, we saw that we received very different responses
when we provided different system messages. This should not come as a surprise to us. After all,
as network engineers, we have spent decades mastering the art of communicating with network
devices through CLI commands. When we open our favorite terminal window and SSH to a router,
we literally open up a “window” of communication to tell the device what we want it to do. In
time, we gradually integrate more communication methods into the device – say, SNMP and API
– but the end goal is still to provide a set of instructions to make the device do what we tell it to do.
Now, with AI LLMs becoming powerful tools in our toolkit, we need to master the way we commu-
nicate with AI models effectively, with prompt engineering. We can think of prompt engineering
as the equivalent of CLI syntax for AI models, except instead of the strict CLI syntax dictated by
the vendor, we use natural language to help AI understand what we need it to do. Just as a poorly
formatted BGP configuration can bring down our network, a poorly crafted prompt can give us
a dangerous AI response.
Often, people think of prompt engineering as a new skill, but it is really about applying existing
network engineering skills to a new type of interface. We need to leverage the same type of sys-
tems thinking and planning from our network engineering background in the new interface to
help the AI model be more effective in solving our problems.
Prompt Engineering for Reliable Outputs 66
In this chapter, we will go over some recipes for constructing effective prompts:
• Giving directions to AI models
• Specifying return formats
• Giving examples
• Providing feedback
• Building prompts gradually
Crafting an effective prompt takes patience and practice – sometimes, we even need to tailor the
prompt toward the specific model we are using. But the recipes covered in this chapter should be
universal, regardless of the model we are using, and provide a good starting point for all queries.
Are you ready? Let’s get started.
Technical requirements

3.1 Giving directions to AI models
Think of an AI model as a newly hired network engineer on their first day; they are capable, but
they need to be “onboarded” with clear directions and instructions.
Getting ready
Please refer to the chapter 1 Recipe 1.1 Getting ready section for this recipe.
How to do it…
1. Create a Python script with a relatively vague prompt:
from openai import OpenAI
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
# Bad example - vague and directionless
vague_prompt = "Help me with BGP configuration"
response_vague = client.chat.completions.create(
model="gpt-4",
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": vague_prompt}]
)
print("Vague Response:")
print(response_vague.choices[0].message.content)
print("\n" + "="*50 + "\n")
2. Execute the script to see the output. Your result will be slightly different:
$ python 3_1_vague_prompt.py
Vague Response:

used for routing between autonomous systems (ASs). The following is
a basic example of how to configure BGP on your router:
Before starting configuration, make sure you have the following

information:
1. Your network's autonomous system number (ASN)
2. The IP addresses of the routers you'll be adding to the BGP
network
```cisco

Router(config-router)#network <network> // Specify the networks that
you want to advertise

of neighbor> // Define a neighboring BGP router and specify its AS

to memory so it stays even after reboot
```

Replace `<ASN>`, `<network>`, `<neighbor IP address>`, and `<AS of
neighbor>` with your actual values.
Remember that each router configuration will be different depending
on your network's topology and size. It's important to have a good
understanding of your network's existing configuration before
attempting to implement BGP.
Please note that configuring BGP incorrectly can have serious
consequences for your network, so always take caution when making
changes and consider consulting with a network specialist if you're
unsure about any steps involved in the process.
Educate yourself thoroughly about BGP and related topics before
attempting to implement it on your network. There are numerous
books, websites, and formal training courses available that can help
you in this aspect.
Consider practicing in a test environment first before applying
configuration changes to production equipment. It's a good idea to

• Defines the scope: We defined a clear scope – that is, Cisco ASR9000 router – the ASN

3.2 Specifying return formats
As we saw in previous recipes, if we want a certain return format, we need to be clear and precise
about it. In the preceding recipe, we asked the prompt to use the IOS-XR format for its response,
which is an example of a ready-to-paste CLI command. By the same token, we can also specify
JSON format for API integration, YAML for a human-readable format, or an Ansible playbook-style
return format.
In this recipe, we’ll experiment with different return formats.
Getting ready
We will need to install an additional Python package, pyyaml, for this recipe. We will also need
to export the OPENAI_API_KEY in our environment variable:
$ pip install pyyml
$ export OPENAI_API_KEY="your-openai-api-key" #This step is only needed if
you did not use the '.env' file.

- Include a summary section with total counts
Provide ONLY the JSON output, no additional text.
"""

model="gpt-4",
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": json_prompt}]
)

print(response_json.choices[0].message.content)

How it works…
Format specification leverages an AI model’s existing knowledge from training. If we were to
perform the same task manually, we might miss a detail or two despite our best efforts; a miss-
ing period or an extra space is not uncommon. The key to the instructions is to do the following:
• Be explicit, such as specifying Return JSON format
• Specify the structure – for example, Group devices by role using YAML groups
• Use format-specific language, such as make it ready to use with ansible-playbook
commands
When it comes to specifying formats, it is helpful to specify no additional text to let the AI
model know we do not need documentation and explanation.
There’s more…
We can also combine a format request with validation instructions:
validation_prompt = """
[your main request here]
Return as valid JSON that passes the following validation:
1. All strings must be properly quoted
2. No trailing commas
3. Include a "validation" field with timestamp
4. Test that json.loads() can parse it successfully
After generating the JSON, mentally validate it against these rules before

3.3 Giving examples
Simply put, the more examples we can provide, the better the AI can understand our needs. In
prompt engineering, concrete examples that we can provide include our organization’s standards,
naming conventions, and best practices.
Let’s consider a newly hired engineer as an example. If we want to have our very capable colleague
configure a router, we would probably get them to reference another similar router, right? “Hey
Bob, take a look at lax-cor-r1 and try to configure lax-cor-r2; they are very similar except for
their loopback interfaces, IP addresses, BGP router-id, and so on.” That is what we mean by
giving examples to AI – we want to give it concrete templates to follow.
Getting ready
This recipe follows the same setup as the previous recipes: make sure the OPENAI_API_KEY envi-
ronment variable has been exported.
How to do it…
1. Start by providing a standard interface description, then ask for an output:

standard.

specific format.
Here are examples of the correct format and style:
Example 1:

Output: interface GigabitEthernet0/1
description UPLINK_TO_SW-DIST-01_Gi0/5_10GB_CORE

Example 3:

description FIREWALL_OUTSIDE_PA3220_10GB_SECURITY
Now, apply the same format and style to this input:

"""

3.4 Providing feedback
At the beginning of this chapter, we discussed treating AI as a newly hired, capable-but-new net-
work engineer colleague. Imagine that you have such a colleague on their first day on the job;
do you expect to give them instructions and be done with them? Of course not – not if we are
realistic about producing the right output. Even if we give the colleague detailed instructions
and examples to follow, we would still expect the process to be iterative. We would sometimes
need to repeat important information. The more complex the problem, the more iterative we
expect the process to be.
It would be helpful to review the first set of results produced by the colleague, give feedback based
on the results, and guide them toward the right solution.
In this recipe, we will learn how to use an iterative process to gradually improve AI responses.
Prompt Engineering for Reliable Outputs 84
Getting ready
Similar to the previous recipes, make sure the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable has been
exported.
How to do it…
1. Create the following script to ensure there’s a two-pass, iterative process for the response:

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
# Initial request
print("=== ITERATION 1: Initial Request ===")

Create a basic access control list (ACL) for our office network.
We need to control traffic between our internal network and the
internet.
"""
response = client.chat.completions.create(
model="gpt-4",
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": initial_prompt}]
)
response1 = response.choices[0].message.content
print("Response:")
print(response1)
print("\n" + "="*60 + "\n")
# Provide feedback for improvement
print("=== ITERATION 2: After Feedback ===")
feedback = """
The previous ACL is too basic. Please improve it with these
requirements:

3.5 Building prompts gradually
As we stated in the preceding recipe, Providing feedback, the prompt engineering process requires
constant feedback. In some complicated cases, we will need to deliberately build up the prompt
gradually in order to not overwhelm the AI LLM tool. Building complex prompts is similar to de-
signing a complex network or studying for a difficult certification exam, such as CCIE. In terms of
creating a design, we would start with a basic technology that aims for connectivity, satisfy the
basic technical requirements (bandwidth and budget), and then layer it with routing, security,
and monitoring. In terms of studying for an exam, as an example, we would start with the basic
topics, then gradually layer the more advanced technologies on top.
If we try to do too much too fast, with the AI LLM, it often leads to confusion and suboptimal results.
In this recipe, we will learn how to construct prompts systematically, layering complexities grad-
ually until we reach our intended goal.
Getting ready
We will use the same OpenAI setup that we did in the preceding recipe.
How to do it…

Chapter 3 93
The key is to realize that AI models are better at doing one thing at a time (just like their human
counterparts) with hierarchical structures.
There’s more…
Once we are comfortable with the separate scripts, we can also combine them into a single script
without losing their hierarchical structure.
The network engineer’s advantage
As with any new technology, one of the most frequently heard questions is, Will this technology
replace my job? I heard this question when network automaton was introduced many years ago:
Will I automate my job away? I also heard a different variation of this question when cloud com-
puting became a mainstay: Will all physical networks become obsolete? However, the question on
everybody’s mind now is, Will AI take away my job?
Many experts predict that the AI revolution is going to be bigger than cloud computing, and
some even argue that it will be bigger than the internet. In that case, it is coming for everyone’s
jobs, not just network engineers’. However, if we consider the previous network automation
and cloud computing example, the network engineer’s role evolves with the new technology;
some functions will be replaced, while other functions will evolve, and some new jobs that we
have not seen before will be introduced. While nobody can foresee the future, I do think network
professionals have a significant advantage, as illustrated by the concepts of prompt engineering
that were introduced in this chapter:
• Network engineering requires breaking down complex problems into logical steps
• Often, network engineers need to specify precise requirements and constraints
• Network engineers need to provide clear examples and documentation
• Network engineering often requires multiple iterations and refined solutions
Do these skills sound familiar? They should, because they are the same skills we discussed in
this chapter that make for good prompts. The same skills that make a good network engineer are
the same that are required for working with AI LLMs when it comes to prompt engineering. The
skills introduced in this chapter are not about replacing your networking knowledge; they are
about amplifying it. As we saw from this chapter’s recipes, providing BGP, VLAN, and security
information significantly improves the time-to-solution with AI’s help.
So, let’s keep our heads up high and learn how to use AI to our advantage!
Prompt Engineering for Reliable Outputs 94
Summary
In this chapter, we learned about the essentials regarding prompt engineering. By using the right
prompt, we can transform AI from a generic helper into a specialized network automation partner
we can all appreciate. Just to recap, we went over giving specific, role-based prompts, specifying
return formats, providing solid examples and feedback, and building prompts gradually in a

step-by-step way.
We should note that prompt engineering is really not a new technology; it involves applying
existing network engineering skills in a new interface – an interface that serves as a gateway to
the AI LLM partner. If we apply the same systematic thinking, precise requirements, and iterative
process that we use for our network engineering skills to working with AI models, we are good to go.
So far in this book, we have mainly been using cloud-based LLMs with API requests. However,
this setup is not always possible in certain environments that require air-gap security or need
to comply with certain government regulations. In the next chapter, we will dive more in-depth
into using local LLMs. See you there!

In previous chapters, we mostly used cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs) with API

solution might not work in your environment:
• Data sovereignty: In certain industries, such as healthcare, financial, and legal, you may
prefer to house your data, including network information, in your environment, despite
the promise of the provider not to use your data for training.
• Compliance requirements: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Health In-

• Cost: Pay-per-token cloud solutions might become expensive over time. In comparison,

to an AI LLM provider.
• Latency: Cloud-based solutions add route-trip latency and delay to each transaction,
which might be prohibitive for real-time applications.
Primarily for the reasons cited, we want to construct a local AI LLM solution for our network
automation effort.

4.4 Using the Llama 2 Uncensored model for
advanced code generation
One of the benefits of housing our own local AI LLM is the freedom to “‘try out”’’ new models.
When we use a hosted model, such as OpenAI or Anthropic, we are using their version of the
sometimes opinionated model. When we house our own models, we get to try out models “‘in
the wild.”’ In this recipe, we will use the Llama 2 Uncensored model for testing.
Some reasons why we might want to use an uncensored model include the following:
• The script generation is unrestricted for complex network configurations
• We might not want any content filtering limitations, such as a security assessment for
authorized penetration testing
• The model will not impose any restrictions on generating code involving sensitive system
details
We will begin by downloading the Llama 2 Uncensored model.
